Nineteen sequences per gene from the GenBank database were added. The Maximum Likelihood (ML) tree returned a topology identifying only one branch in the two genes analysed, thus grouping all three species, and with the Assemble Species by Automatic Partitioning (ASAP) and Poisson Tree Processes (PTP) analyses we obtained the same result. Considering the possibility that the diversification process probably occurred rapidly and relatively recently, these markers do not result in the reconstruction of phylogenetic relationships. Therefore, other genes with a higher evolutionary rate give better answers for understanding phylogenetic relationships in this group and for assessing the species composition and richness contained in this ecosystem.

The genus Etmopterus Rafinesque, 1810 comprises small to medium-sized (<800 mm TL) bioluminescent sharks that inhabit the deep ocean (> 200 m) and are popularly known as lanternsharks. Currently, 43 valid species are recognised, which can be classified into four groups based on shared synapomorphies and analyses of nuclear and mitochondrial genes. In the western South Atlantic, five valid species are recorded: E. bigelowi Shirai & Tachikawa, 1993; E. gracilispinis Krefft 1968; E. granulosus (Günther, 1880); E. hillianus (Poey, 1861); and E. lucifer Jordan & Snyder, 1902. Thus, within the scope of the Projeto Diversidade e Evolução dos Peixes de Oceano Profundo –DEEP-OCEAN, the objectives of this work are to investigate, on the basis of morphological and molecular characters, the species richness of the genus in this region. The material used was obtained on the Brazilian continental slope and includes 36 specimens with tissue samples for molecular work, collected aboard the R/V Alpha Crucis; 36 specimens obtained as bycatch of commercial fishing in São Paulo; and 64 specimens from national and international ichthyological collections. For the molecular evidence, the mitochondrial genes COI and NADH2 were used. The subclass Holocephali (Chondrichthyes) includes about 60 extant species of primarily benthopelagic fishes found in all the world's oceans, mainly between 200 and 2,500 m depth. The group is diagnosed by a relatively elongate body with a large head and pectoral fins, ventral mouth, six tooth plates without continuous replacement, the presence of spines anterior to the dorsal fins, and lateral line segments forming exposed grooves on the head and along the body, among other characteristics. Chimaeras also have quite evident sexual dimorphism in the adult stage, with males possessing claspers formed from modifications of part of the pelvic fins, as well as tenacula associated with the anterior region of the head and the prepelvic region. The extant forms of Holocephali are grouped in the families Chimaeridae, Callorhinchidae and Rhinochimaeridae. Rhinochimaeridae includes the genera Harriotta Goode & Bean 1895 (3 species), Neoharriotta Bigelow & Schroeder, 1950 (3 species), and Rhinochimaera Garman 1901 (3 species). Rhinochimaera atlantica Holt & Byrne 1909 is a relatively rare species, with scattered records throughout the eastern and western Atlantic. The few records of the species in Brazilian waters come from grey literature or from publications that make no explicit reference to specimens deposited in scientific collections. In this study, we present preliminary data on the anatomy of an adult female specimen (721 mm TL) of R. atlantica collected in 2008 in the Campos Basin, RJ, at approximately 1,200 m depth (NPM 868). The measurements and counts of this specimen are within the variation reported in the literature, including the number of caudal tubercles (about 32), which are structures present along the dorsal margin of the caudal fin that are typically less developed in females of the genus. Additional observations on the geographic distribution of R. atlantica in the western South Atlantic are also presented.

This survey therefore shows the potential of social media for mapping ghost fishing in Brazil as a tool for monitoring cases, raising awareness and engaging users as citizen scientists.

Microcosm experiments were conducted using autoclaved silty loam soil, mimicking the shallow layers of the Bennington series of soils, with shed skins and Oo conidia added to treatment groups. A control group without shed skins was used for comparison. After several weeks, fungal growth was analyzed using qPCR to quantify fungal DNA. Results will provide insights into how shed skins within den sites may allow spores to persist in the environment, potentially acting as reservoirs for Oo. Understanding the environmental factors that contribute to the longevity and transmission of this fungal pathogen is crucial for snake conservation, particularly for species like the timber rattlesnake. This research may help inform targeted interventions, such as treating den soils, to reduce the spread of Oo and prevent further declines in vulnerable snake populations.
2938: Studies in teleost behavior and social structures have, for the most part, been relegated to freshwater and reef systems, while ignoring inter- and subtidal fishes. Our study examined the social behavior of the penpoint gunnel (Apodichthys flavidus), a sub-tidal fish commonly found along the West Coast of the United States. We quantified location preference and behavioral reactivity based on factors such as predator presence (Myoxocephalus polyacanthocephalus), conspecific presence, and availability of a structural hide. We observed a lack of reaction when in the vicinity of a predator species and significant differences in quadrant preference based on the previously mentioned factors. There were significantly fewer aggressive social behaviors (i.e., striking and pursuing) when a similar-sized conspecific was present compared to a larger conspecific. Interestingly, focal individuals were also likely to share a rock shelter with both similar-sized and larger conspecifics despite previous negative interactions. There also appeared to be social preference between focal fish pairs, with one pair exhibiting predominately non-aggressive behaviors (i.e., tangling and bumping) and frequent physical contact, whereas the other focal pair exhibited more aggressive behavior towards one another. Our results suggest that A. flavidus exhibit advanced social behavior that may be influenced by their ecology and habitat preferences, as well as behaviors that are likely beneficial to their survival.
2939: The purpose of this project is to research the breeding habits and egg development of Plethodon petraeus. This salamander's range is an estimated 10 square miles on and around Pigeon Mountain in northwest Georgia. P. petraeus are only found in the limestone gulfs and cave entrances on Pigeon Mountain. According to the IUCN Red List, they are listed as a “near threatened species,” showing the importance of studying this species. This presentation highlights two studies providing insight into the Pigeon Mountain Salamander. The first is Tim Herman's successful research with P. petraeus laying eggs in captivity. His enclosure simulated seasons through light and temperature changes, and eggs were laid on a moist rock with water running slowly over them. This re-creation was a sufficient replication to the salamander's natural habitat to lay eggs. The second study highlights John Jensen’s work concluding that their breeding could occur in the late spring and early summer and egg-laying in late summer to early fall. In other research he observed the closely related Plethodon glutinosus guarding a clutch of eggs suspended from the top of a crevice in a cave. This presentation concludes by proposing a study using borescopes to search crevices for clutches of eggs, much like the observations of P. glutinosus.  Knowledge of the Pigeon Mountain Salamander's breeding habits, including egg deposit sites and development, is important for keeping the species from going extinct. I hope the results from this study will encourage breeding programs in zoos, keeping this species alive.
2940: Amphibians include anurans (frogs and toads), caudates (newts and salamanders), and caecilians. Amphibians are an integral part of any ecosystem performing valuable services from controlling populations of pests as well as providing a source of protein for human consumption in many parts of the world. About 41% of the world’s amphibians are threatened with extinction due to multitude of threats such as infectious diseases; climate change; habitat degradation and loss, and habitat fragmentation due to infrastructure development. Even many amphibian species with the least conservation status are showing decreasing population trends. In Pakistan, amphibians are represented by 21 species belonging to four families: Bufonidae, Megophryidae, Microhylidae, and Dicroglossidae. This study was conducted to examine genetic variation in the uncommon frog (Sphaerotheca maskyei), samples were collected from natural and degraded habitats, DNA was extracted from tissue samples (toe clips) and sequenced for the 16S rRNA (mitochondrial gene) and RAG 1 (nuclear gene).   The genetic analysis revealed that all samples collected during the present study formed a clade with Sphaerotheca maskeyi which confirmed the species. Based on 16S gene, S. maskyei is found to have a high haplotype diversity (natural: haplotype number (N)=1, haplotype diversity (Hd)=0.96; degraded: N=4, Hd= 0.76); low nucleotide diversity (π) (natural= 0.06, degraded=0.06) showing recent divergence form a common ancestor or population expansion with insufficient time for mutation to accumulate; excess of rare alleles and population expansion, higher mutations but with low frequencies (natural: Tajima’s D= -2.43, degraded: D= -1.54) which is also confirmed by Fu and Li’s F values (natural= 0.99, degraded=0.67, P> 0.05) showing no strong evidence of deviation from neutrality. Results of AMOVA revealed low genetic differentiation (FST : 0.10, P=0.07) where only 10% genetic difference is due difference among populations and the rest (90%) of the genetic variation occurs within populations. Based on RAG 1 gene, S. maskyei is found to have a high haplotype diversity (natural: N=4, Hd=0.98; degraded: N=4, Hd= 0.67); high nucleotide diversity (π) (natural= 13, degraded=50) showing a population where mutations are accumulating; excess of rare alleles and population expansion, higher mutations but with low frequencies (natural: D= -1.26; degraded: D= -0.05) which is also confirmed by Fu and Li’s F values (natural= 0.89, degraded=0.67, P> 0.05) showing no strong evidence of deviation from neutrality. Results of AMOVA revealed low genetic differentiation (FST : 0.014, P=0.07) where only 1.47% genetic difference is due difference among populations and the rest (98.5%) of the genetic variation occurs within populations
2941:
Infrastructure development ranks among the top three threats to amphibians worldwide, driving habitat fragmentation and ecosystem modification. Despite its global significance, empirical data on these impacts remain scarce for many amphibian species.  This study investigates habitat fragmentation in the Himalayan foothills, and evaluates the influence of specific factors on the occurrence of endemic frogs in fragmented landscapes, utilizing Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) data for 2022 and projected trends for 2030. Our findings reveal that certain study sites within the Murree-Kotli Sattian-Kahuta National Park support endemic species such as Nanorana vicina and Allopaa hazarensis, while the Margalla Hills National Park supports amphibian species with globally declining populations, including Euphlyctis adolfi, Sphaerotheca pashchima, and Microhyla nilphamariensis. A strong positive correlation (r = 0.94) was observed between vegetation cover and the protection status of the sites. LULC projections indicate significant urban expansion, leading to vegetation loss within protected areas, with unprotected sites experiencing even higher rates of urbanization and vegetation decline. Among the models tested, the model endemic status ~ vegetation showed the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and was selected as the best fit. Vegetation cover was found to be the strongest predictor of endemic species occurrence (Likelihood Ratio Test: χ²(1) = 4.699, p = 0.031). Our study has filled a research gap and provided evidence that habitat fragmentation resulting from residential and commercial development, natural system modifications and subsequent ecosystem degradation affect vegetation and influence occurrence of endemic species in the Himalayan foothills.

Keywords: Endemism, Decreasing population, Invasive, Infrastructure development, Attrition, Firth’s logistic regression
2942: Whale catfishes (family: Cetopsidae) are most well-known from two abundant, widespread species that are commonly referred to as “giant candiru.” These two species (Cetopsis coecutiens and C. candiru) are infamous for their voracious appetite, being often encountered burrowing into dead or dying fishes caught in gill nets and in some cases even preying upon humans, both living and deceased (Valente-Aguiar et al., 2020). Despite this reputation, very little is known about feeding habits and capabilities of the remaining members of this family, although a few of the earliest branches within this family are known to be primarily insectivorous. We present here a comparative study of feeding morphology and functional constraints across the Cetopsidae. We CT scanned 35 species across all valid genera of Cetopsidae. We input and rendered reconstructed CT data files using the software 3D Slicer, and then measured traits from teeth, oral jaws, and pharyngeal jaws that have been hypothesized to be important to feeding. We used dimensionality reduction techniques to further explore correlated traits that may be associated with the dietary transition observed in giant candiru, and to further hypothesize on the diets of those cetopsids lacking reliable dietary data.
2943: Using the gene Cytochrome oxidase subunit 1 (CO1), we created a DNA barcode library for the reptiles and amphibians of Chicagoland, specifically focused on the Will County Forest Preserves. To date, we have sequenced 24 species of reptiles and 13 species of amphibians, for a total of ~800 CO1 sequences across all taxa. The construction of this database accompanies a larger resurvey effort for the overall documentation of the herpetofauna of Will County, and it will supply a reference library for future projects to draw from. This library will expand existing knowledge on genetic diversity of reptiles and amphibians within the county. Furthermore, this work aims to examine the relationship of genetic diversity and how it correlates to habitat connectivity in the region, which has wider application to maintaining natural corridors between heavily fragmented forest preserves nestled within urban settings to preserve biodiversity.
2944: Urbanization has altered the hydrology and vegetation structure of many remaining wetlands in the United States. Hydrological and vegetation shifts can alter food availability and disrupt food chains, thus impairing energy flow among trophic levels. For wetland species to persist in altered habitats, managers should promptly develop strategies prioritizing the most vulnerable populations. In some cases, land managers must evaluate population health using short-term data, which can be difficult with long-lived turtle species due to extreme longevity and delayed sexual maturity. Body condition indices (BCI) are commonly used as proxy measurements of body fat, which are assumed to reflect foraging success and fitness of individuals. Body condition can change rapidly in response to resource availability, disease, and stress, making it a viable surrogate for assessing short-term population health. A population with significantly lower body conditions may indicate chronic stressors or fewer site resources. The two extant Spotted Turtle (Clemmys guttata) populations in Illinois inhabit sites within a heavily urbanized landscape and previous studies revealed differences in demography and microhabitat composition. Here, we compare body conditions between the two remaining populations of Spotted Turtles in Illinois as an additional measure of population health.
2945: Rattlesnakes are widely killed where their habitat overlaps with humans, increasing the risk of bites and challenging wildlife conservation. Fear, disgust, and knowledge have been shown to predict the moral acceptability of killing snakes. Project RattleCam was founded in 2020 to improve perceptions of rattlesnakes while engaging community scientists in studying their ecology. We created a science curriculum for third through fifth graders called RattlEd to amplify Project RattleCam’s impact on young audiences. RattlEd aligns with Next Generation Science Standards, engaging students as scientists in a range of activities including studying snake behavior using the livestream, creating models, playing games, and engineering a wildlife crossing. We evaluated how the RattlEd curriculum changes student knowledge and perceptions of snakes using a tripartite survey that students complete before and after the RattlEd unit. The survey asked students to draw a moment in a rattlesnake’s day, write a short paragraph describing their drawing, and answer three Likert-style questions about how much they like, fear, and are disgusted by rattlesnakes. Student drawings were manually coded by researchers, and ATLAS.ti also analyzed the themes and sentiments of the students’ descriptions of their drawings. All RattlEd lesson plans, teaching materials, and science notebook activities are available at RattleCam.org. We hope this curriculum will serve as a model for engaging students in community science while fostering empathy and understanding for misunderstood wildlife.
2946: Chytridiomycosis, caused by the fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd), is a major infectious disease contributing to the decline of amphibians worldwide. While the most severe losses have been observed in Central and South America, the impact of Bd on Africa’s amphibian fauna remains uncertain. Opportunistic surveys indicate that Bd is widespread across the continent but without clear evidence of large-scale mortality. In addition, research in other temperate and tropical amphibian communities has demonstrated that both abiotic (e.g., temperature, precipitation) and biotic (e.g., host identity) factors can contribute to host-pathogen dynamics and disease outcomes but these hypotheses have not been rigorously tested in African amphibian communities. We conducted a multi-year standardized survey of Bd at the Bouamir Research Station, located in the Dja Biosphere Reserve in Cameroon. This rich amphibian biodiversity area is representative of lowland Central African rainforests and serves as an ideal site for long-term monitoring. The study involved bi-monthly surveys along 20 transects in various habitats (forests, swamps, watercourses) over a two-year period. Captured individuals were identified, photographed, and screened for Bd using quantitative PCR techniques. Individuals of the three most abundant genera (Arthroleptis, Leptopelis, Phrynobatrachus) were uniquely marked to enable detection of recaptured individuals and long-term monitoring of infection status. To understand which factors contribute to host infection status we present our results of Bd prevalence and infection intensity across the amphibian community with respect to seasonality (precipitation and temperature), life history (direct developing species versus those with a biphasic life cycle), and proximity to streams. Our results present an important contribution towards understanding host-pathogen dynamics in a hyper diverse community of African amphibians.
2947: As urbanization continues to grow, construction and other efforts are causing an unnatural increase in sedimentation and turbidity of waterways. Studies have consistently shown that varying levels of turbidity can impact various fishes' behaviors in many ways, which can pose some concerns about the implications of turbidity on overall aquatic ecosystems and fish biodiversity. Simple alterations to fish behaviors, such as to hunting and antipredator responses, could impact a freshwater ecosystem over a long period of time. Turbidity impacting foraging and hunting success could be a big indicator of a species’ success in an ecosystem. This project aims to explore the impacts of various turbidity gradients on the foraging and feeding behaviors of various freshwater fishes found in the Savannah River basins in Georgia and South Carolina. Species found in the Savannah River basins, such as many Etheostoma darters, have had limited representation in recent discourse, especially regarding turbidity and its impact on their foraging behaviors. Sediment from local rivers and lakes will be used to create turbidity gradients across several tanks, and local freshwater fishes’ foraging behavior for live food will be observed over a period of time. The fishes kept in turbid environments will be compared to a control group of fishes kept in clear water. The results of this project will fill in some of the gap that exists in research on the effects of turbidity gradients on several species of Savannah River freshwater fishes’ foraging and feeding behavior.
2948: The family Pomacentridae is a widespread, species-rich group of primarily marine fishes, commonly found on tropical and subtropical reefs around the world. The family is best known for the anemonefishes, which form obligate symbiotic relationships with anemones. Currently, there are over 400 recognized damselfish species divided among 29 genera and four subfamilies. Sequence data from a fragment of the mitochondrial control region (~500–600 bp) were collected and analyzed with data from previously published mitochondrial (12S, 16S, ATPase 8/6, cytochrome b, cytochrome c oxidase I) and nuclear (histone 3, recombination activating gene 1, and tmo-4c4) genes. These sequences represented over 350 damselfish species, including all 29 genera. The topology recovered by maximum-likelihood analyses supports the phylogenetic relationships found by other recent studies. The family, all four subfamilies, and most genera were resolved as monophyletic groups.
2949: Amphibian populations have experienced substantial global declines in recent decades. Blanchard’s cricket frog (Acris blanchardi), a small, semi-aquatic, member of the family Hylidae was once abundant throughout the midwestern United States, ranging from as far south as Texas and Louisiana and extending north to Michigan and could also be found in Ontario, Canada. Since the 1970s, A. blanchardi populations have been declining especially in the northernmost regions of their range. Despite past efforts investigating various possible drivers of the decline, there are still no clear links between environmental change and the species current distribution. To address this shortcoming, we used ecological niche modelling (ENM) to assess historical, current, and future suitable habitat availability for A. blanchardi. Modeling was accomplished using maximum entropy (MaxEnt) with species occurrence data collected from natural history collections databases and the iNaturalist community science platform combined with bioclimatic variables sourced from WorldClim. By identifying key environmental factors and mapping suitable habitat, this research expands our understanding of the habitat requirements of A. blanchardi and will inform future conservation efforts.
2950:
We will present the NSF BIO-LEAPS Advisory Board's response to the changes the American Elasmobranch Society (AES) made based on their 2024 recommendations. The poster will address ongoing issues of inclusivity and accessibility within shark research. It will review the Advisory Board's proposed  recommendations to foster a more inclusive environment and report on AES' progress towards implementing these recommendations. Key goals include revising AES’s policies and guiding documents to ensure a welcoming atmosphere, introducing diversity training and a train-the-trainer model, and providing resources to facilitate change in similar organizations.

Some of the recommended changes have been implemented, such as improvements to the Gruber Award criteria and symposia transparency. However, deeper changes, including revisions to AES’s bylaws, code of conduct, and ethical guidelines, are still needed to ensure long-term inclusivity. The Advisory Board calls for these structural changes to address barriers that hinder participation, such as socioeconomic and accessibility concerns, and to enhance diversity within leadership positions.

The Advisory Board emphasizes the importance of implementing comprehensive diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) training and strengthening the Code of Conduct and Code of Ethics to protect marginalized groups and ensure accountability. Additionally, improvements in accessibility, including wheelchair access, sign language interpreters, and dietary accommodations, are crucial for ensuring that AES events are fully inclusive.
2951: The Beartooth Butte Formation includes Early Devonian (Lochkovian-Pragian) deposits from 419 to 394 million years old and has been thoroughly studied from a paleobotanical perspective, including reconstruction of the depositional environment. However, the fishes of this assemblage have scarcely been addressed since the work of Bryant in the 1930s. A team from Cal Poly Humboldt collected numerous bony plates of placoderm and ostracoderm fishes from the Cottonwood Canyon outcrops of the formation (~405 Ma, Wyoming), and these are now deposited in the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH) Fossil Fish Collection, with some scattered material co-occurring with fossil plants  temporarily housed at Cal Poly Humboldt. Additional Beartooth Butte material is housed at the Field Museum of Natural History (FMNH). We assessed the shape and ornamentation of numerous fish plates from Cal Poly Humboldt and the AMNH, adding at least six new species to the Cottonwood Canyon assemblage that had previously been known solely from the type Beartooth Butte locality in Montana. Various cephalaspidomorph ostracoderms are present, as well as early arthrodire placoderms and a relatively three-dimensionally preserved cranial region of a single specimen. In addition to identification of isolated fish plates and description of an articulated specimen, the three-dimensional fossil was CT scanned at the AMNH and we digitally reconstructed its anatomy. Combining CT scanning with traditional preparation and macro photography provides a fresh look at the fishes of Cottonwood Canyon, 90 years after Bryant’s initial observations.
2952: Freshwater Drum, Aplodinotus grunniens (Sciaenidae), is a widely distributed, understudied freshwater species endemic to North and Central America. It occurs throughout much of the central and eastern United States and southern Canada, extending southward to southern Mexico and northern Guatemala. Despite its commonness and widespread distribution, little is known about intraspecific genetic variation across its native range. Therefore, this study aimed to analyze the genetic diversity of A. grunniens across its geographic range. We obtained 43 samples from Great Lakes (Lake Michigan-Fox River), upper Mississippi River, Pearl River, San Jacinto River, Sabine River, Neches River, Colorado River (TX), Rio Grande, and the Grijalva–Usumacinta River basins. We used double-digest RAD (ddRAD) sequencing to genotype single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from each sample. Population diversity and structure were estimated from the SNP data using a suite of population genetic and phylogenetic methods. The results from this study provide an initial overview of the demographic patterns, genetic diversity, and phylogeographic history of Freshwater Drum populations across their range.
2953: The micronucleus (MN) assay is a commonly employed genotoxicity test used for detecting DNA damage resulting from exposure to chemical pollutants and other environmental stressors. MN are small, chromatin-containing round bodies visible in the cytoplasm of cells, which can represent chromosomal fragments resulting from un- or mis-repaired DNA strand breaks and/or small extrachromosomal bodies formed from genomic instability. The MN assay is routinely used in fish toxicity studies because it can be easily performed using peripheral blood smears due to the occurrence of nucleated erythrocytes in most non-mammals. However, to date, very few studies have attempted to use the MN assay for detecting genotoxic responses in elasmobranch (sharks, skates, and rays) erythrocytes. In addition, no studies have examined whether staining procedures influence the sensitivity of this test in elasmobranchs despite evidence for overreporting of MN in bony fish erythrocytes prepared using routinely employed procedures. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to evaluate the use of the MN assay in elasmobranchs. To accomplish this, we examined baseline levels of MN in blood smears from a common elasmobranch species, the sandbar shark Carcharhinus plumbeus. We also compared MN measurements in C. plumbeus blood smears prepared using the commonly used but often inaccurate Giemsa staining approach with the DNA-specific Feulgen stain. The results of this study showed low levels of MN present in C. plumbeus erythrocytes. Furthermore, while Giemsa-stained cells exhibited higher numbers of MN, average differences between MN numbers in Giemsa-stained and Feulgen-stained blood smears did not differ significantly.
2954: Aquatic invasive species cause detrimental effects to native fish populations and economic resources. Bigheaded carp (Silver Carp Hypophthalmichthys molitrix and Bighead Carp H. nobilis), are two such species present in Nebraska’s water bodies. Originating from eastern Asia, they were brought to the United States in the early 1970s for aquacultural use. They have since expanded and established populations in the Missouri River basin, the mainstem Platte River, and major tributaries to the Lower Platte River. The reproductive potential of bigheaded carp is a topic of interest as conservation efforts have focused on best removal and control practices. Unfortunately, little is known about the potential reproductive changes in response to shallower water systems typical of the Platte River. This study aims to fill knowledge gaps on the spawning phenology and magnitude across the hydrologically distinct Platte River basin to better understand the reproductive potential of Silver Carp and Bighead Carp in similar shallow-water prairie systems. Methods of fish collection include the use of electrofishing boats, fyke nets, and seines, and reproductive potential will be assessed using meristic and histological techniques. Results of our 2025 and 2026 sampling seasons may inform us of seasonal changes in reproductive readiness, verification of spawning events, and fecundity of individuals in the lower Platte River and its tributaries. This data will allow comparison to bigheaded carp reproduction in deeper-water systems and aid research managers in developing invasive species management regimes in Nebraska that are biologically sound, logistically feasible, and amenable to public perception and support.
2955: Fluctuating asymmetry (FA), the deviation from perfect bilateral symmetry, serves as a measure of developmental instability influenced by environmental stressors. Amphibians, particularly Blanchard’s Cricket Frog (Acris blanchardi), are effective bioindicators due to their sensitivity to habitat changes. This study aimed to assess FA in A. blanchardi populations across three sites in the Dayton, Ohio, area to evaluate its potential as a bioindicator of habitat quality. Fieldwork conducted from May to August 2024 yielded 70 frogs, with habitat and water quality data recorded at each site. Hindlimb asymmetry was measured using ImageJ software, and statistical analyses included ANOVA and a one-tailed t-test. Results showed no significant variation in FA across the sites, but a significant difference between sexes, with males exhibiting higher asymmetry than females. These findings suggest that biological factors, such as sexual dimorphism, may play a greater role in FA than anticipated. The lack of significant environmental effects highlights the need for further research into how different factors interact to affect FA. Potential future research will expand sample sizes to look into these other factors and strengthen FA’s utility as a conservation tool for amphibians.
2956: The well-documented collapse of highland Central American amphibian communities at the end of the twentieth century was fundamental to the discovery of the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) as an agent of global amphibian declines. Mass die-offs were taxonomically and ecologically selective, but post hoc phylogenetic assessments of extinction risk are complicated by a lack of frozen tissues for taxa that disappeared. Because thorough genetic inventories of pre-decline communities do not exist, we used DNA sequence data derived from 60-year-old formalin-fixed museum specimens to test a hypothesized relationship between the extinct golden toad (Incilius periglenes) and two critically endangered highland congeners that also suffered contemporaneous declines. We obtained whole mitochondrial genomes for multiple individuals of all three species and verified resulting assemblies with independent extractions of different tissue types. Combined with a preexisting molecular dataset of extant Incilius, we find strong support for a monophyletic clade of highly susceptible montane endemics. Our results underscore the substantial phylogenetic diversity preserved by surviving members of the clade and suggest that some components of Bd susceptibility in this group derive from common ancestry.
2957: Molecular phylogenetic studies can help show the evolutionary history and relationship among species, which are important for understanding biodiversity and ecological dynamics. This research aims to examine variation in the mitochondrial genome across species from the family of Acanthuridae, a group of fish that are ecologically important for maintaining the algae on coral reefs. This group of fish includes surgeonfish, tangs, and unicorn fishes. By analyzing publicly available mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences, this research aims to reconstruct the phylogeny of Acanthuridae based on partial mtDNA genome sequences to reconstruct their evolutionary histories and better understand processes shaping their diversification. Using bioinformatic techniques in combination with publicly available databases allows us to make the most out of data originally published for an alternative purpose. These species also are at high risk due to climate change and human activity. Understanding the evolutionary history and phylogeny of these fish is important for conservation efforts, especially since they play a vital role in coral reef ecosystems.
2958: The genus Sphenomorphus as currently constituted is a large (115 spp.) and diverse group of lizards distributed throughout Australasia. Sphenomorphus has long been considered a “catch-all” taxon, with similar-looking but taxonomically difficult species being placed in the genus. Previous research has focused on morphology, but recent molecular data from the Philippines has shown morphological characters to be convergent and the genus to be polyphyletic. The island of New Guinea is known for its high vertebrate biodiversity and has been shown to have unprecedented numbers of cryptic species yet to be described. Despite this, little research has been done in New Guinea, resulting in a knowledge gap of many groups, including Sphenomorphus. We present phylogenetic analysis within New Guinean Sphenomorphus using multiple mitochondrial and nuclear gene regions. Preliminary results support the non-monophyly of Sphenomorphus, as well as multiple currently recognized species. New Guinean Sphenomorphus are not monophyletic, with some taxa falling within the Eugongylini. While biogeography is outside the scope of this project, multiple dispersal events are found, hinting at the complex biogeographic history of this group.
2959: The invasive hemlock woolly adelgid (HWA) has decimated Eastern and Carolina hemlock populations in the Southern Appalachian Mountains. Imidacloprid, a neonicotinoid insecticide, is currently used to suppress HWA populations and conserve hemlock trees and the habitats they create. Concerns have emerged about possible non-target impacts of imidacloprid use on amphibians, including salamander populations, due to the insecticide’s ability to persist in soils and leach into streams. Recent research in our lab found evidence that increasing imidacloprid dose in forests reduces stream-breeding salamander terrestrial but not aquatic abundance. We hypothesize that imidacloprid may be having subacute effects on salamanders exposed in streams as larvae. Through field sampling and controlled exposure experiments, we assessed the potential for imidacloprid accumulation in the brain and effects on behavior and brain morphology of larval Nantahala Black-bellied salamanders (Desmognathus amphileucus) and Blue Ridge two-lined salamanders (Eurycea wilderae). By examining the risks posed by imidacloprid to stream salamanders, our research will contribute to forest management decisions that need to balance invasive species control, hemlock conservation, and amphibian conservation.
2960: Shortfin Makos, Isurus oxyrinchus, are lamnids that have a global distribution in temperate and tropical oceans. Locations of critical early life history events including mating, birthing, and nursery areas are unknown or unconfirmed for most populations. The objective of this study was to identify a nursery area for Shortfin Makos in the northern waters of the Mid-Atlantic Bight using the criteria articulated by Heupel et al. (2007). Satellite tags were used to track the movement of juveniles ­(<200 cm TL, n=7) up to 5 months. Tag detections (n=882) confirmed that young makos stay in continental shelf waters of the northern Mid-Atlantic Bight off Long Island, NY USA, through the meteorological summer (June–August) and early meteorological fall (September–October) when sea surface temperatures are between 18–23°C. There was clear migratory movement from juveniles once sea surface temperatures fell below 15°C. During late fall, some young sharks moved south towards Cape Hatteras while one shark moved east up to 1,800 km into the open north Atlantic Ocean into meteorological winter. These movement data of juvenile Shortfin Makos combined with multi-year catches and sightings (2018–2024) provides strong evidence for a nursery area in the northern Mid-Atlantic Bight. By identifying a nursery area for Shortfin Makos, we can help close knowledge gaps that currently exist for this vulnerable species and support effective management.
2961: Ecotourism and community science are increasingly popular conservation techniques used to engage the public with native ecosystems and influence future human behaviors regarding wildlife. Marine wildlife encounters, such as snorkeling and diving, are a prime example of ecotourism and community science activities that are – in part – justified through opportunities to promote human behavioral changes while generating scientific data on understudied and elusive species. Since 2015, the Vermilion Sea Institute has been using photo mark-recapture to identify whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) in Bahía de los Ángeles, Mexico with the help of community science volunteers. Despite the apparent abundance of whale sharks in this region, much is still unknown about their population demographics or survival. We used a Cormack Jolly Seber (CJS) model to estimate whale shark survival and detection probability using encounter data from 2015 to 2024. We then compared our estimated population survival and composition to similar whale shark studies. We expected that survival and population demographics may be influenced by the high density of commercial fishing in the Gulf of California. Key findings from the study show that (1) the predominant demographic of this study area is juvenile male individuals, (2) detection probability is 4.87% ± 0.5%, (3) survival probability is 97.8% (4) there is a negligible difference in survival rates between sexes, (5) as size increases by one foot, survival probability increases by 1.5685 (logit scale). The Vermilion Sea Institute will be able to use the findings of this study to better understand the status of whale sharks in the Bahía de Los Ángeles area and inform future ecotourism practices while collaborating with local conservation agencies to improve species protection.
2962: Snakes have undergone many major evolutionary events instrumental in their current success: complete limb loss, decoupling skull structures enabling larger prey consumption, and development of specialized feeding structure in the form of fangs. Fangs are enlarged teeth that facilitate venom injections for prey capture. Fangs enabled multiple prey capture strategies and facilitated high diversity in fanged (colubriform) snake skull morphology. While this skull diversity has been identified, the cause is still a mystery. Ecological variables such as diet and habitat have been explored, but many factors have yet to be considered. Our goal is to evaluate factors affecting colubriform skulls. We sampled 149 species across five major colubriform families from museums and previous scans from the public database Morphosource. We quantified skull variation for museum specimens using micro-CT scans and created 3D meshes with fixed landmarks in Slicermorph which were transformed with a local superimposition. We obtained foraging, diet, and habitat data from previous literature and databases. We used geometric morphometric methods to investigate ecological variable effects on skull morphology, modularity, integration, disparity, and evolution rates of skull structures. We observed diet and foraging mode having significant effects on the ectopterygoid and maxilla. While these structures are affected by diet and foraging mode, it seems that the ontogenetic changes in snakes are the most likely cause of diversity, as the ontogenetic modularity hypothesis has the most support from modularity testing and multiple skull structures follow historically described ontogenetic trends of positive allometry, structural rotation and dorsal-ventral flattening of the braincase.
2963: The Lower Florida Keys has been identified as an important area for multiple species of teleosts and elasmobranchs. In recent years, the area has been experiencing unprecedented marine environmental challenges. In late 2023 and early 2024, fishers and researchers began reporting an ‘anomalous spinning fish’ condition throughout the Lower Florida Keys. This condition has been documented to affect a number of teleost and elasmobranch species and initial findings suggest that neurotoxins produced by the algae Gambierdiscus could be linked to the spinning fish behavior. The physiological impacts for elasmobranchs is still uncertain. Our study aims to investigate the potential sublethal physiological impacts of this condition for coastal sharks in the area. Blood panels of Negaprion brevirostris, Carcharhinus limbatus, and Ginglymostoma cirratum were analyzed for a variety of metabolites and biomarkers to assess physiological condition. Samples were collected prior to, during, and following the peak of the reported ‘spinning event’ allowing us to conduct a preliminary comparison of these markers across time. This study provides insight to how this anomalous environmental condition may impact local shark stocks, if the impacts perpetuate, and determine if adjustments to local conservation management efforts may be warranted in the future.
2964: Adult phenotypes result from dynamic interactions among developmental stability mechanisms and developmental instability. Among the stability mechanisms, modularity has been targeted as a primary evolutionary developmental component facilitating the evolvability of complex systems. Among the various definitions of modularity is the concept that a module is a network of interacting elements behaving as quasi-independent units, or as semi-autonomous sets of highly correlated traits within larger units. Here we explore the modular organization of the Weberian apparatus (WA) among key cypriniform taxa. This complex system (WA) consists of a series of anterior centra, neural arches, supraneurals, and pleural ribs that form a mechanical linkage transmitting motion of the swim bladder to the inner ear. For this study, micro-CT technology and 3-D geometric morphometrics are employed to test for modularity of the anterior vertebrae with respect to more posterior vertebral regions. We also investigate, via principal-components analysis, covariation among elements within the Weberian apparatus. Results of this study demonstrate that the Weberian apparatus in cypriniforms is a functional module. Covariation of individual elements within the Weberian apparatus differs among cypriniform groups, resulting in the evolution of morphologically distinct submodules as evidenced by phylomorphospace analysis. Differences among the submodules in various cypriniform groups reflect differing ecological habitats and adaptations.
2965: Amazonian Ecuador exists in contradiction. Its biodiversity is a powerful cultural monument far beyond the boundaries of the rainforest. However, the national economy relies on its extraction through oil drilling and ecotourism. Conservation biologists bear first-hand witness to this ecological destruction and its complex socioeconomic context but are expected to remain unfeeling and objective towards it, despite the deep love they develop for their study organisms and the environment through their work. These relationships are intensified for Ecuadorian herpetologists, who must contend with a cultural disregard for herpetofauna, particularly in an age of global amphibian population decline. This project contests the harsh (perceived) separation between the natural sciences and emotion, expanding on our understanding of climate action and the unconventional forms of care between conservationists and abjected animals. I conducted participant observation and 20 semi-structured interviews with herpetologists throughout Amazonian Ecuador and Quito over a month. Their relationships with the reptiles and amphibians they study reveal a careful balancing act between maintaining standards of professionalism and holding a profound, personal love for these organisms; both sides of this quandary inform choices that weigh care for individual organisms against a commitment to broader species conservation. My interlocutors emphasized that the greatest impacts of their work were not felt in “technical” science but in the power of outreach efforts that help their communities develop a love for reptiles and amphibians, despite the stigma. Their labor generates conversations about a biocentric and agentive climate future achieved, step-by-step, in our ecological present.
2966: The ability to possess camouflage capabilities can play a vital role in a species’ ability to obscure their position while they sneak up on prey or limit visibility from potential predators. There are various strategies for camouflage in marine habitats, such as using cryptic coloration to blend in with the environment or to muddle an individual’s silhouette. The need for camouflage presents a challenge for species living in the open ocean, including pelagic sharks (Selachii), where there is little physical habitat structures for them to use for camouflage. As a result, most pelagic sharks rely on camouflage associated with light either produced from the sun or themselves. This selective pressure drives two primary forms of camouflage in pelagic sharks: countershading and bioluminescence. Both methods functionally produce a lighter ventral surface that can blend in with downwelling light, and a darker dorsal surface that can blend in with the dark water below when visualized from above. In this study we explore the evolution of camouflage patterns across all species of sharks, with a primary focus on pelagic species.
2967: Amphibian research in Cameroon has predominantly focused on montane regions along the volcanic line, leaving the more diverse and ecologically complex lowland rainforests poorly understood. The Dja Faunal Reserve, the largest protected area in Cameroon and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lacks comprehensive studies on its amphibian diversity, with no existing checklist of species. This gap is concerning given the critical role of amphibians as bioindicators of ecosystem health and the urgent need for baseline data to inform conservation efforts in the face of habitat degradation and climate change. We aimed to document amphibian diversity in the reserve, investigate habitat and microhabitat influences on species distribution, and create the first comprehensive checklist for the area, thereby advancing knowledge of Central African rainforest amphibians and supporting conservation strategies. We conducted systematic surveys across 20 transects in two distinct habitat types: terra firme forests (≥50 m from streams) and swamp/stream habitats (≤1 m from water). Transects were sampled on three consecutive nights during bimonthly field campaigns from April 2022 to April 2024, covering both dry and wet seasons. We recorded species richness, abundances, and microhabitat use, while measuring environmental variables such as leaf litter moisture, habitat temperature, leaf litter depth, and canopy cover. Amphibians were photographed, identified morphologically, and tissue samples for a subset of individuals were collected for taxonomic verification via DNA barcoding of the 16s mitochondrial gene. Our results reveal exceptional amphibian diversity, with 45 species recorded so far, representing 17 genera and 10 families across two orders (Anura and Gymnophiona). Most species are lowland rainforest specialists, currently classified as ‘Least Concern’ on the IUCN Red List. We observed distinct differences in species composition and abundance between terra firme forests and swamp/stream habitats, highlighting the influence of microhabitat characteristics on amphibian diversity. Seasonal variation was also evident, with higher species richness and abundance during the wet season. These findings position the Dja Faunal Reserve as a critical protected area for amphibians in Central Africa, laying the groundwork for future research and conservation efforts in this globally significant ecosystem.
2968: Islands are natural laboratories for rapid evolution given their typically small founding populations and unique selective pressures relative to the mainland. Accordingly, insular taxa often diverge adaptively from their mainland relatives. The Northern Channel Islands experience substantially cooler air temperatures than adjacent coastal Southern California. Consequently, endemic Island Fence Lizards (Sceloporus becki) experience cooler temperatures than their mainland thermophilic sister taxon, Western Fence Lizards (S. occidentalis). Have Island Fence lizards shifted their thermal physiology to compensate for lower island temperatures? We will determine whether cooler island climates have selected for adaptive thermal shifts in Island Fence Lizards. There is a strong correlation between regional climate and thermal traits in S. occidentalis, yet no studies exist for S. becki. We hypothesize the microniches of S. becki will be cooler than those of S. occidentalis during the activity season, thus requiring greater thermal efficiency and selecting for lower thermal preferences, tolerances, and temperature-dependent performance. We predict an east-to-west gradient of adaptation, with west-most San Miguel Island the coolest-adapted populations. Preliminary field body temperatures (n = 151) support this prediction. As the climate warms, ectotherms like lizards that have adapted to cooler temperatures may be especially vulnerable. Our results will have important implications for the management of this insular endemic. Habitat-restoration projects are underway for other Channel Island endemics, but we lack knowledge of the thermal biology or microhabitat requirements of S. becki to develop similar plans. Additionally, our project will shed light upon how insular ectotherms evolve to compensate for climactic variation.
2969: Blue spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale) are a common species native to the Great Lakes region that, outside of the breeding season, largely remain underground in burrows or under logs. The species is common, yet poorly studied because it is fossorial. To better understand soil habitat choice and burrowing ability, I examined how differences in substrate impact behavioral responses. I used three circular choice arenas (630cm2), each containing four different substrates. Two trials were conducted; the first had each salamander in the arena for 48 hours in darkness, while the second trial had a 12:12 LL:DD photoperiod, with observations made during the light phase. I observed the substrate each salamander inhabited and its behavior (e.g., burrowing, resting on top of the soil). Results indicated that salamanders chose humus in Arena 1 70% of the time, and perlite/topsoil 70% of the time in Arena 3. They never selected sand or humus/topsoil, suggesting an avoidance behavior under light:dark photoperiods compared to darkness. Additionally, salamanders exhibited three times more burrowing behavior under light:dark conditions. In contrast, under darkness, the salamanders did not make any statistically significant selections in soil choice in any of the three arenas. Overall, we conclude that exposure to light impacted soil preference and burrowing frequency. Our findings suggest that salamander exposure to light conditions, perhaps including during surface migration, may cause differences in soil selection and habitat choice.
2970: The family Bagridae (Bleeker 1858) is a widely dispersed clade of catfishes comprised of 225 species belonging to 15 Asian genera and one African genus. Nomenclatural credit is attributed to Bleeker’s 1858 tribe Bagrini, although the group is thought to have been first conceptualized with Cuvier’s 1816 “les Bagre.” Since its inception, Bagridae has been a revolving door of taxa due to the use of plesiomorphic characters in early diagnoses. Taxa belonging to 17 present-day catfish families have been variably assigned to Bagridae under different definitions of the group. Our current understanding of the Bagridae is based on morphological systematics from the most recent revision of the family by Mo in 1991. Though a few bagrids have been included in order-level analyses, there has been no dedicated molecular study of the Bagridae at the family level. Monophyly of the modern Bagridae has yet to be validated. Phylogenetic analysis of molecular data available on GenBank shows that current sampling is insufficient to address this problem. Only 126 bagrid species are represented on GenBank, of which only 35 are sampled at genomic or even mitogenomic scales and the remainder are largely represented by one or only a few single gene sequences. Additional tissue samples reflecting broader taxonomic sampling are required to facilitate a genomic approach to inferring the bagrid phylogeny. Here we present our current understanding of a molecular phylogeny of Bagridae and ask for contributors and collaborators on a more complete work to resolve the relationships of this long-overlooked catfish family.
2971: This study explores the evolutionary history and biodiversity of the Central African frog genus Trichobatrachus (hairy frogs), with a focus on the discovery of potential new species within this group. Trichobatrachus is renowned for its unique physiological traits, including bony claws and hair-like structures in males, which make it a compelling subject for evolutionary and conservation research. Despite its growing recognition, the taxonomy of Trichobatrachus remains unresolved, with species boundaries and cryptic diversity still under investigation. Using a multidisciplinary approach, this research combines morphological analysis, genetic sequencing, and niche modeling to assess species boundaries, polyploidy, and evolutionary relationships within Trichobatrachus. Preliminary findings suggest the presence of previously unrecognized species within this genus, which appear to be geographically distinct and exhibit significant morphological variation, including differences in sexual dimorphism and limb proportions. These variations could suggest ecological adaptations to stream-dwelling habitats. This species description, informed by both field and museum specimens, documents the diagnostic morphological traits that distinguish these potential new species, including snout-vent length, head width, and limb proportions. These traits are crucial for taxonomic identification and advancing our understanding of the ecological roles of Trichobatrachus in its native habitats. The findings contribute to herpetological taxonomy, species conservation, and the management of biodiversity in Central Africa’s changing ecosystems.
2972:
Blue-spotted salamanders (Ambystoma laterale; BSS) are mole salamanders and spend a large

portion of their lives underground. In late March to early April, they travel from their

subterranean habitats to freshwater pools to reproduce. The BSS population on Presque Isle,

Marquette, MI faces challenges when migrating. Ecotourists come to witness their migration

across the road and their path is lit by street lamps and bright lights. Spectators will often

illuminate the salamanders using cameras or flashlights. We investigated how BSS responds to

light conditions in different wavelength and intensity environments with light choice arenas

(direct light, indirect light or complete darkness) when different color filters were applied. Results

indicated that choice of BSS light condition did not differ significantly across color options, with

darkness remaining the preferred condition. However, data revealed that the implementation of

red and blue light filters more than doubled the amount of individuals willing to engage with

lighted areas. The use of red or blue color may present as an effective strategy for harm

reduction of this species.
2973: Human-driven climate change is causing global ecological destruction. Notably, the introduction of environmental pollutants and increased water temperatures in aquatic habitats is causing fish populations to experience behavioral and developmental changes, including the emergence of deformities of the spine and vertebrae. In turn, impaired development of the spine can reduce fish fitness by worsening swimming capacity and potentially compromising typical body shape, an adaptively important trait associated with a population’s lifestyle and habitat. While temperature is known to influence the development of the spine, it is not well understood how temperature-induced spinal deformities impact external body shape. Here, we describe how temperature-induced spinal anomalies influence the body shape of the Mexican tetra (Astyanax mexicanus). Vertebral fusions, vertebral compressions, vertebral curvatures, and anomalies of the hemal and neural spines were identified in 888 A. mexicanus specimens reared in the lab under different temperature treatments. Geometric morphometrics will be employed to determine the body shape changes associated with spinal anomalies of different categories, quantities, and locations. Based on preliminary data, we anticipate significant shape changes associated with each anomaly type and affected region; in particular, we expect a trend of deeper bodies in individuals with vertebral compressions and the greatest body shape divergence in individuals with hemal and neural anomalies.
2974: The genus †Coccolepis is a rare and enigmatic extinct ray-finned fish (Actinopterygii) found in Jurassic and Cretaceous geologic marine and freshwater deposits from around the Earth. Much regarding †Coccolepis remains understudied, including its evolutionary history and relationships, biogeography, diet, and ecological niche. Two fossil specimens on loan to St. Cloud State University preserve jaws and teeth of two possible species of †Coccolepis. These jaws show unique dentition along the upper jaw margin, with teeth near the posterior section curving towards the front of the mouth. This anteriorly-curved dentition is uncommon in fishes. Each specimen also displays differences in the shape and size of the teeth present, as well as the shape of the maxilla bone, indicating that these are likely two distinct species. We examine and describe these unusual jaws and teeth, with the possibility of identifying them to a particular species or determining if they represent new species of †Coccolepis. We will compare these teeth to similar dentition found in living or fossil fishes in hopes to better elucidate a potential diet, niche, and purpose for anteriorly curved teeth in the posterior portion of the jaw. By understanding the potential diet of †Coccolepis, we may gain a better understanding of how fishes evolved and adapted to novel trophic niches that were opening up during the breakup of Pangaea and the changing planet.
2975: The southeastern coast of the United States represents an important habitat for multi-species complexes of elasmobranchs, including juvenile sharks. Estuaries serve as essential environments for the early life stages of several species. This study investigates the temporal patterns and abundance of juvenile sharks from 2021 to 2025. Samples were collected from three Georgia estuaries—Wassaw, Ossabaw, and Doboy Sound. Bottom-set longline surveys were conducted with a standard 50-hook set for a 30-minute soak time. Once captured, sharks were identified to species, measured (lengths and mass), sexed, tagged and released. The four most abundant species were Sphyrna tiburo (bonnethead shark), Rhizoprionodon terraenovae (Atlantic sharpnose shark), Carcharhinus limbatus (blacktip shark), and Carcharhinus plumbeus (sandbar shark). Of the 13 shark species identified, abundance varied from hundreds to as few as two individuals, highlighting the dynamic nature of these estuaries and differential use by species. We also examined the capture rate for each species to assess daily abundance to investigate variation among species spatially and temporally within estuaries. Patterns observed provide insight about when and how different species of sharks use estuaries, which can inform conservation efforts aimed at mitigating human impacts and supporting the long-term sustainability of juvenile shark populations.
2976: Papua New Guinea is a known biodiversity hotspot and is home to some of the most diverse frog fauna in the world, including the majority of species found in the Austro-Papuan tree frog subfamily Pelodryadinae. Difficulties in sampling this region and in differentiating species that are morphologically cryptic have resulted in many species remaining undescribed. DNA barcoding has been demonstrated to be an effective technique for the preliminary identification of cryptic species within poorly understood groups. We present a molecular phylogeny of Pelodryadinae based on the universal barcode COI and compare multiple single locus species delimitation methods (GMYC, sPTP, and ABGD) with morphological species delimitation. We find that as currently described the genera Litoria, Nyctimystes, and Ranoidea are paraphyletic, and demonstrate that regardless of the method used, there are many undescribed cryptic species. Within the 32 morphological species analyzed, our results identify from 51-63 total species based on the method of delimitation used. Additional molecular, morphological, and ecological data is necessary to fully describe the diversity of Pelodryadinae.
2977: In 2024 and 2025 abnormal spinning fish behaviour has been observed throughout the Florida Keys and South Florida. Fish that exhibit this behaviour are unable to maneuver properly and have been found swimming in repeated circles. The exact cause of ‘spinning’ is unknown but has been linked to physiological impairment and has resulted in mortalities for several teleost and elasmobranch species. Whether the occurrence of this behaviour is impacting the relative abundance of species within this area has yet to be determined. To address this question, we examined fisheries-independent longline surveys conducted in the Lower Florida Keys from 2022-2025. Catch rates were dominated by coastal shark species including Negaprion brevirostris, Ginglymostoma cirratum, Carcharhinus limbatus, and Carcharhinus acronotus. The catch rate and relative abundance for several species was lower during the peak of the anomalous spinning fish events in 2024 but has moderately rebounded in 2025. Monitoring is continuing in order to determine long-term trends and potential recovery.
2978: Human-mediated dispersal has influenced the geographic distributions of organisms for at least 20,000 years. Due to their variable geological characteristics and human histories, island systems provide opportunities to study the combined impacts of both natural and human-mediated movement. The California Channel Islands have never been connected to the mainland and have been occupied by humans for at least 13,000 years. On these islands, several alien species have become established as a result of human-mediated dispersal, including the iconic island fox. The Common Side-blotched Lizard (Uta stansburiana) occurs on five of the eight Channel Islands, and previous work suggests at least three distinct mainland-to-island colonization events are responsible for their current island distribution, with one occurring in the last century. Genomic methods provide promise for their ability to help resolve the complicated histories of island inhabitants, including the timing of colonization and divergence events. I am generating a SNP library from 650 U. stansburiana individuals on mainland California and the Channel Islands. Using coalescent modeling, I will infer the most likely times of divergence between island and mainland populations, as well as population growth, gene flow, and changes in effective population size through time. My research will determine the role of natural versus human-mediated dispersal in the establishment of U. stansburiana on each island. This work will contribute to our understanding of how ancient and contemporary human populations influence the distribution of organisms on island systems and will inform the management of this and other island taxa.
2979: It is well known that among many marine organisms the accumulation of toxic pollutants increases in top predators because of biomagnification. Many studies have demonstrated that sharks are among the marine predators that often exhibit the highest concentrations of marine pollutants. One of the most notable pollutants is the toxic, non-essential metal mercury (Hg), which has been shown to be elevated in many different shark species; however, much still remains unknown about Hg accumulation in several commercially and recreationally important sharks on the U.S. east coast. This study examined the levels of Hg accumulation in U.S. east coast sandbar sharks, Carcharhinus plumbeus, a common but still poorly studied species with regards to Hg exposure. This study presents temporal trends in Hg levels in Atlantic coast sandbar sharks over a 40-year period (1986-2024), demonstrating a decline in Hg accumulation likely associated with reductions in Hg emissions rates. The study also examined spatial differences in Hg accumulation in Atlantic and Gulf sandbar sharks from recent years. These data demonstrate that, despite long-term declines in Hg accumulation, muscle Hg levels in sandbar sharks from some regions still remain above federal thresholds for human consumption.
2980: Endocrine analysis is an important tool for examining the physiology of chondrichthyans. For example, measurements of the gonadal steroid testosterone can be useful for evaluating sexual activity in male sharks and rays, allowing researchers to determine reproductive timing and breeding locations. However, assessment of hormone cycles generally involves extended period of animal restraint and the collection of blood samples, which can often be difficult to perform with some elasmobranchs, especially larger species and/or those sensitive to capture stress. With these points in mind, we examined the effectiveness of using small fin biopsies for the use in measuring gonadal steroid hormone patterns in chondrichthyans, focusing on the measurement of testosterone in male Atlantic sharpnose sharks Rhizoprionodon terranovae, a well-studied species for which reproductive endocrinology has already been well-characterized. Immature and mature male R. terraenovae were collected from FL, GA, and SC estuaries using bottom longline fishing and small fin biopsies were collected nonlethally using routine procedures. Samples were washed to remove mucus and other contaminants, minced, and hormones extracted using methanol following procedures previously described for use with other vertebrate tissues, including teleost scales, crocodilian scutes, and mammalian nails and hair. Hormone extracts were dried under air, reconstituted in buffer, and assayed for testosterone using chemiluminescent immunoassays. Testosterone concentrations in fin biopsies increased in male R. terraenovae with size, showing significant increases in mature males in comparison with young-of-year and juvenile individuals as well as immature and mature females. Fin testosterone concentrations also showed temporal increases in mature males corresponding with known periods of increased mating activity in spring. These results suggest that hormone analysis of fin biopsy may provide a new tool for evaluating hormone cycles and related physiological processes in chondrichthyans.
2981: Salamander larvae exhibit a high degree of phenotypic plasticity. Their external gills, which enhance respiratory surface area, vary significantly with environmental conditions. Previous studies suggest that low-water flow promotes the development of larger gill structures. To investigate this, we raised Ambystoma mexicanum larvae in both high- and low-flow environments. Using a novel imaging method, we quantified gill size and complexity from both frontal and dorsal perspectives. We hypothesize that larvae in high-flow conditions develop smaller gills because the energetic costs of maintaining large gills may outweigh their benefits in oxygen-rich environments. We also predict that larvae returned to a low-flow environment will regenerate larger gills, though this ability may depend on prior acclimation to low-flow conditions. This study provides insight into the plasticity and reversibility of gill morphology in response to environmental changes, contributing to our understanding of respiratory adaptations in aquatic amphibians.
2982: Axolotls (Ambystoma mexicanum) exhibit highly plastic external gills that play a crucial role in respiration. Past studies have primarily measured gill branch length as an indicator of gill development, yet this method may not fully capture the complexity of gill morphology. Gill structure is three-dimensional, and branch length alone may overlook variations in branching patterns and overall gill arrangement. In this study, we compared gill morphology using both dorsal and lateral perspectives to assess whether traditional measurements accurately reflect gill complexity. By employing a novel imaging approach, we analyzed gill branch arrangement and overall structure from multiple angles. We hypothesize that gill complexity is better represented by a combination of measurements rather than branch length alone and that different perspectives highlight distinct morphological traits. This study provides a more comprehensive framework for assessing gill plasticity and respiratory adaptations in aquatic salamanders.
2983: Emerging diseases and human-induced climate change pose a global threat to wildlife. Ectothermic species are particularly vulnerable to environmental changes due to thermally constrained activity patterns. While the decline of Eastern Diamondback Rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus; EDB) populations has been widely attributed to anthropogenic activity, further research is needed to address how environmental pressures drive behavior, which can inform predictions regarding species-level resilience. Disease susceptibility and environmental influences (i.e., temperature, precipitation) on reproductive phenology make gravid females a particularly vulnerable demographic due to the physiological demands of reproductive cycles. Using datasets from two isolated coastal populations, we examined the effects of biotic and abiotic predictors on daily and seasonal activity patterns of EDBs. Using logistic regression, our goal was to examine the effects of environmental conditions, reproductive condition, and disease on phenology, surface activity, and ecdysis cycles. We hypothesized that winter surface activity and shortened brumation periods would be associated with increasing temperatures. Additionally, we hypothesized that individuals with skin lesions suggestive of ophidiomycosis (also known as snake fungal disease) concurrent with the detection of Ophidiomyces ophidiicola would express increased ecdysis frequency and winter surface activity. Lastly, we expected that geographically distinct populations would differ in phenology and surface activity. Our investigation will improve our understanding of population-level vulnerability and processes that drive population decline.
2984: The Guana and Tolomato rivers provide essential habitat to several ecologically and economically important species, including serving as nursery habitat to a variety of shark species, most notably the scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini). Spanning the Northeastern Florida coast, they are home to over 50 endangered or threatened species and hosts several habitat restoration projects due to the rivers’s ecological significance. Due to their proximity to developed areas along the coast, they can be threatened by human influences, such as pollution. While the negative effects of human interaction with the environment are of growing public interest, the effect of pollution in the Guana and Tolomato rivers has not been well studied. Therefore, the overall purpose of this project is to examine pollutant exposure in species residing within the Guana and Tolomato rivers, specifically that of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). PFAS have been shown no clear pattern of accumulation or biomagnification in marine ecosystems and pose significant health risks to marine organisms and the humans that consume them. This presentation will discuss preliminary PFAS data in a variety of shark species and their prey, including sandbar sharks (Carcharhinus plumbeus), bull sharks (Carcharhinus leucas), and scalloped hammerheads. These results will be analyzed in conjunction with stable isotope data and be compared to Maximum Contaminant Levels in drinking water as identified by the EPA.
2985: Invasive species are an ongoing concern to our natural world and pose a unique threat to aquatic ecosystems. Amphibians are especially vulnerable to stressors imposed by invasive species. For this study we will investigate direct and indirect impacts the invasive plant species amur honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) and tree of heaven (Alianthus altissima) may be having within aquatic ecosystems using small-mouthed salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and American bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) as model organisms. In addition, we will use American bullfrogs as a model organism for amphibian invasion and investigate their impact on small-mouthed salamanders. 36 cattle tank mesocosms have been setup to mimic ponds found in the midwestern United States. Treatments have been assigned to 28 of the 36 tanks, allowing for 8 control tanks. Small-mouthed salamander tanks received one of five treatments: addition of amur honeysuckle, addition of tree of heaven, addition of bullfrogs, addition of amur honeysuckle and bullfrogs, or addition of tree of heaven and bullfrogs. Bullfrog tanks received one of two treatments: addition of amur honeysuckle or addition of tree of heaven. The results for this experiment are pending, but we predict that both species of amphibians will experience increased mortality and decreased body mass at metamorphosis when exposed to the invasive leaf litter. We also predict small-mouthed salamanders in the presence of bullfrogs will have decreased body mass at metamorphosis
2986: Stable isotope analysis has long provided insight to feeding ecology, habitat use, and physiological status in chondrichthyan fishes. Recent work quantifying the isotopic composition of organic material bound within the mineralized portions of shark teeth has suggested that teeth of different ages (i.e., sampled from different rows) may preserve ecological chronologies given that they represent different temporal windows. As such, teeth from individuals associated with more isotopically homogenous environments, such as pelagic species, should exhibit more constrained isotopic variability than coastal species. This prediction has not been robustly tested across a diversity of species and is required to refine estimates of functional plasticity. We quantified δ13C and δ15N variation in organic material extracted from teeth by measuring those of different ages and positions across jaws from individuals associated with different habitats. Specifically, we explored whether isotopic variation observed across shark teeth of adult bull (Carcharhinus leucas, coastal Indian Ocean), adult dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus, pelagic Indian Ocean), and juvenile white (Carcharodon carcharias, coastal California) sharks is consistent with the diversity of habitats encountered throughout life. Initial analyses of bull shark teeth show high δ13C variation (-17.7 to -10.0‰) and lower δ15N variation (9.8 to 12.4‰) expressed across the jaw. We also observed isotopic shifts across teeth, from older to younger, possibly indicating habitat transitions between pelagic and coastal environments. These and related findings using the dentine component of teeth will support novel assessments of functional plasticity in both modern and historical contexts given the potential application to museum specimens.
2987: Accurate measurements are critical data for managers in the study of wildlife. Measuring animals in the wild, such as  marine megafauna can be difficult, especially for species that cannot be directly measured without invasive capture techniques, this includes the giant manta ray (Mobula birostris). The Florida Manta Project aims to assess and compare different measurement methods: 1) underwater laser photogrammetry, 2) aerial photogrammetry, and 3) visual estimation by trained researchers.
