This study compares the precision of these methods by analyzing measurements of 20 mantas collected during small boat surveys. The primary objective is to identify potential discrepancies in size estimates between the methods and assess the variation in measurements. These findings will provide insights into the reliability of these commonly used methods and contribute to refining measurement protocols for marine megafauna research. Ensuring the precision of size measurements will enhance the understanding of manta ray life history traits, such as size at maturity, supporting more effective population models and conservation strategies.
2988: Streams are important habitats for amphibians in Northeastern Pennsylvania, which are reliant upon these water sources for their larval development and adult survival. Prescribed fire, a practice that is used to manage forest undergrowth, often occurs in regions where there are streams. Whereas direct stream habitat may not be burned, runoff from burned habitat could likely impact streams. This study was done to determine how prescribed fire affects the water chemistry of various stream habitats and biodiversity of salamander species. Changes in the water chemistry and biodiversity were documented in six streams within burnt, and unburnt, lands located in Northeastern Pennsylvania. pH, turbidity, and total dissolved solutes were recorded at each of the streams. Three 100-ml water samples were collected from each stream and analyzed in a laboratory for heavy metals, particularly lead, cadmium, arsenic, copper, and zinc. The high heat of a fire could release heavy metals from bound states in the soil humus and plants in the form of ash runoff. Salamander biodiversity at each stream was determined by conducting time-constrained surveys over the course of several months. Alpha and beta biodiversity were compared among burned and unburned sites using population data collected from each survey. Differences in water chemistry were determined between burned and unburned sites. Our results will help determine if prescribed fire has any impact on the water chemistry or salamander biodiversity of streams
2989: Lamniformes (Elasmobranchii) is a relatively small but diverse shark order, consisting of seven families, ten genera, and fifteen species. Although the dental morphology of these sharks is well known, the morphological range of their jaws has been poorly investigated. In this study, we quantitatively examined the jaw curvatures of the fifteen lamniform species based on radiographic (X-ray and computed tomography) data using two-dimensional geometric morphometrics. Our study shows that, whereas Alopias spp. exhibit a wide range of jaw curvatures with seemingly no specific pattern, plots of species belonging to the genera Odontaspis, Pseudocarcharias, Carcharias, Lamna, Isurus, and to a certain extent, Mitsukurina are clustered closely together in one morphospace and are characterized by tightly curved jaws. On the other hand, plots of the remaining taxa, Megachasma, Cetorhinus, and Carcharodon, are more widely distributed in another morphometric region and are characterized by broad, gently curved jaws. The former cluster is characterized by conventional piscivorous taxa with narrow, non-serrated piercing-type teeth, whereas the latter is represented by taxa with either large, broad, and serrated cutting-type teeth (Carcharodon, which its gently curved jaw presumably promotes the ‘sawing effect’ of its teeth) or diminutive teeth due to planktivory (Megachasma and Cetorhinus). Phylogenetically, our study indicates that tightly curved jaws are plesiomorphic, and more gently curved jaws are apomorphic. Although the exact reason is unclear, the broad plot distribution for Alopias spp. may be related to their unique hunting strategy using their elongated tail where their jaw curvature may play little role in their feeding.
2990: Sand tigers, Carcharias taurus, are mackerel sharks with a disjunct global distribution in tropical and temperate seas. In the Northwest Atlantic, sand tigers migrate along the coast of the eastern United States from the Gulf of Maine to Florida and occupy structurally complex benthic habitats. The long-term, underwater camera installation, SharkCam, at Frying Pan Tower, off Cape Fear, North Carolina, USA, sits atop an expanse of hard bottom reef frequented by sand tigers. The citizen-science platform, Spot A Shark USA (SAS USA), uses images of sand tigers to identify and track individuals. This study utilized image encounters from SAS USA (n=1,359) and SharkCam (n=3,846) to glean information about sand tiger relative abundance, site fidelity, seasonality, and fish associates off the coast of North Carolina. To investigate site fidelity of sand tigers, SharkCam encounters were entered into SAS USA (n = 545). Sand tiger seasonality, sex, and relative abundance at Frying Pan Tower were tracked from 2014–2021. SharkCam and SAS USA encounters were used for identifying fishes associated with sand tigers. At Frying Pan Tower, 44 individual sand tigers were resighted up to 15 times over multiple years, with some females possessing visual markers of pregnancy. There was a total species richness of 17 fishes behaviorally associated with sand tigers. This study contributes to existing evidence that coastal North Carolina is important for sand tigers throughout their lifetimes, while the understanding of fish associates provides additional insight into interspecific interactions within the food web.
2991: Brevetoxins, the toxins produced by the harmful algal bloom known as Florida Red Tide (Karenia brevis), and their incorporation into elasmobranch tissues is greatly understudied. The only study to date found a correlation between the frequency of red tide blooms and the average concentrations of brevetoxins in elasmobranch tissues collected from animals who experienced a Red Tide-induced fatality (Flewelling, 2010). We utilized competitive ELISA analysis in samples of Blacktip sharks (Carcharhinus limbatus) collected between 2019 and 2024 within Sarasota Bay, Tampa Bay, and Manatee River using bottom longlines and gillnets to further investigate brevetoxin concentrations in blacktips not currently experiencing an active Red Tide bloom. Preliminary data suggests there is a difference between brevetoxin concentrations in tissue types, as well as variation existing between individuals. There is also evidence of a correlation between the time post-bloom and the concentration of brevetoxins. The build-up and elimination of these toxins at sublethal doses in elasmobranchs requires further study, and this project seeks to provide a better understanding of this topic and the impacts of Florida Red Tide on sharks.
2992: The Baja Coachwhip (Masticophis fuliginosus) is a large colubrid restricted to the Baja Peninsula (Mexico) and southern California (USA). Understanding the processes that have led to the current patterns of biodiversity throughout the Baja Peninsula has been the focus of many studies, yet the evolutionary history of this species is poorly understood. Previous work within Baja has suggested that sea level rise, mountain uplift, and desertification have resulted in genetic divergence across codistributed species. Here, we have collected 73 specimens from across the distribution of M. fuliginosus as well as the closely related M. piceus in southern California. We used low-coverage whole genome sequencing to assemble complete mitochondrial genomes. These data were used to construct phylogenies using maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference to infer the evolutionary relationships among whipsnakes and assess the influence of potential geographic barriers on the genetic structure of M. fuliginosus across Baja. Our findings support previous hypotheses regarding the strong influence of allopatric divergence on creating genetic diversity in the southern Baja Cape region; however, we find no population structure throughout the central and northern regions of the peninsula. These data can inform patterns of isolation by distance and environment, which is a key to disentangling the evolutionary history of this species. By using low coverage genome sequencing, we have documented the drivers of diversification within the Baja Coachwhip and suggest that similar patterns may be found in other codistributed squamate reptiles.
2993: Minorities in Shark Sciences (MISS) is collaborating with community members in North Carolina to investigate how sharks use coastal and inland waters in and around Pamlico Sound. This project originated through the efforts of the community-driven Instagram page, Encounter NC, where local shark enthusiasts shared encounters and fostered curiosity about local shark populations. Recognizing the need for deeper scientific understanding, Encounter NC partnered with MISS to explore these sharks more extensively. Pamlico Sound, previously overlooked, has now been identified as a potential northernmost nursery for bull sharks along the U.S. Atlantic coast, extending beyond the previously known boundary of the Indian River Lagoon in Florida. The project also offers a unique opportunity to study the impact of climate change on shark populations. Understanding these shifts is essential for conserving these populations. By integrating community science, satellite tracking, and self-reported encounter data, this project will support local efforts to co-manage Pamlico Sound and the surrounding area and ensure the protection of shark populations, particularly bull sharks, highlighting the crucial role of community engagement in marine conservation. We will present preliminary data from this project as well as the inclusive conservation framework we will employ for the project.
2994: Biofluorescence occurs when an organism absorbs shorter and then emits longer wavelengths of light. Most studies on biofluorescence focus on documentation, rather than on its possible evolutionary function. This study examines the potential ecological significance of biofluorescence in larval Gray Tree Frogs (Dryophytes chrysoscelis/versicolor). Tadpoles in this group develop large, orange-red tails to deflect invertebrate predators. Their tails also fluoresce in the orange-red spectrum. If biofluorescence in tadpoles varies with the predator community, then it could function in signal enhancement for predator deflection. We quantified fluorescence, the invertebrate predator community, and the underwater light environment experienced by tadpoles. We tested 47 tadpoles for fluorescence in response to blue (440 - 460 nm), cyan (490 - 515 nm), and green (510 - 540 nm) light. We used both spectrometry and digital photography to quantify fluorescent emissions and the proportion of the tail fluorescing in the orange-red spectrum, respectively. Biofluorescence varied across individuals. Blue and cyan light, which are present in the water column, produced striking orange-red fluorescence. Proportionally, this fluorescence contributed approximately 0.24 to total brightness under blue and cyan excitation. For some individuals, nearly 45% of the lateral surface of the tail fluoresced orange-red. We use linear models to explore the relationship between site-dependent variables, such as predator diversity, on the orange-red fluorescence of tadpole tails. Our work adds to a limited pool of knowledge regarding biofluorescence in larval amphibians and provides insight into another possible function of biofluorescence in these vertebrates.
2995: Blacknose sharks (Carcharhinus acronotus) and sandbar sharks (C. plumbeus) are two endangered shark species found within the Western North Atlantic Ocean, including in the waters near Miami, Florida.  This study assessed the reproductive biology of mature blacknose (n=56) and sandbar (n=42) sharks captured in the Miami area between December 2019 and December 2024.  We examined plasma concentrations of testosterone (“T”), progesterone (“P4”), and 17β-estradiol (“E2”), and compared those hormone levels to catch date, catch location, season, and gravidity (determined via ultrasonography).  In addition, this study scored mating wounds identified in sandbar sharks using a four-stage wound healing analysis to determine the wounds’ apparent age and compared results of mating wound analysis with location, hormone, and ultrasound data to provide a more complete picture of sandbar shark mating and reproductive activity in the Miami area. Via these components, seasonal variations in levels of T and E2 were identified in blacknose sharks, and circulating E2 levels were correlated with gravidity.  In sandbar sharks, seasonal shifts in T and P4 were identified, as well as a possible relationship between the presence of mating wounds and levels of P4.  These findings provide insight into blacknose and sandbar reproductive biology and seasonality in waters near Miami, Florida.
2996: Spatial capture-recapture is a promising method for estimating population vitals and has been used in many studies on population dynamics. These studies are important because they improve understanding of how species respond in different environments. The eastern red-backed salamander, Plethodon cinereus, is a terrestrial, lungless salamander that is common in Eastern North America and parts of Canada, ranging from Quebec to North Carolina. Plethodon cinereus is small in size and can be easily found and studied in forest ecosystems. This species will defend their territory through aggressive behavior and are known to be territorial. However, the extent of territoriality of males and females, and how salamanders spatially disperse has not been thoroughly examined in Pennsylvania. The goals of this study are to (1) estimate population density and (2) describe differences in (a) spatial distribution and (b) movement patterns between males and females of P. cinereus in central Pennsylvania. We used spatial capture-recapture methods to address these goals and test the following hypotheses. We hypothesized that (1) males have larger foraging areas than females and (2) both sexes display site fidelity by staying within the same plot and area within plot. Our study location included 6 plots of 50 coverboards each in central Pennsylvania where this species has previously been found. Individuals were marked with a unique four-color code through injection of Visible Implant Elastomer tags.
2997: Road salt intrusion and invasive honeysuckle are increasing ecological concerns in freshwater habitats. Amphibians are sensitive to these stressors due to their permeable skin. Salinization can lead to increased mortality, behavioral changes, and reduced growth. Invasive honeysuckle (Lonicera maackii) has been found to cause mass mortality in amphibians. Road salt and honeysuckle are likely to overlap in habitat near ephemeral pools, such as disturbed and edge habitats, which are utilized by amphibians. If these stressors were to synergistically interact, it could lead to a higher increase in mortality and behavioral changes. These negative impacts could ultimately lead to a shift in amphibian community dynamics. We investigated the synergistic effects of road salt and honeysuckle on the predator-prey interactions of small-mouthed salamanders (Ambystoma texanum) and gray treefrogs (Hyla versicolor). Larval A. texanum (predator) and H. versicolor tadpoles (prey) were placed in cattle tanks with a control, honeysuckle, salt, or combined treatment. Half of the cattle tanks contained only A. texanum larvae and the other half contained both A. texanum larvae and H. versicolor tadpoles. Survivorship of H. versicolor tadpoles and A. texanum was monitored along with A. texanum body length, mass, and time to metamorphosis. We found that road salt and honeysuckle did not significantly impact metamorphosed A. texanum life history traits. However, we found that road salt significantly impacted some life history traits of larval A. texanum. Additionally, A. texanum predation ability was not impacted by road salt or honeysuckle.
2998: The role of progesterone (P4) in elasmobranch reproduction has long been under question, as P4 is generally not elevated during pregnancy, unlike in mammals, reptiles, and amphibians.   Numerous previous studies on elasmobranch reproduction, including previously presented results on the bonnethead shark (Sphyrna tiburo), have confirmed that E2 stimulates the production of vitellogenin (Vtg) in the liver during follicular development, but the role of P4 in this process remains undetermined.  This study specifically looked at the potential role of P4 in regulating Vtg production in S. tiburo.  Immunoblotting was used to detect the presence of Vtg in S. tiburo plasma, while chemiluminescent assays analyzed plasma P4 concentrations.   Immunohistochemistry was also conducted to look for E2 and P4 receptors in S. tiburo liver.  Receptors for both E2 and P4 were detected in S. tiburo liver, suggesting both hormones play a role in Vtg production.   High concentrations of plasma P4 were found during the late spring months, when Vtg presence in plasma samples was declining.  These preliminary results suggest that P4 may bind to receptors in the liver and trigger the slowing or termination of Vtg production and follicular development in S. tiburo.  Further investigation of this potential role is needed, perhaps by examining in vitro and/or in vivo effects of P4 treatment.
2999: Tooth morphology and arrangement are widely used in paleontological and ichthyological field guides to identify sharks in the order Lamniformes. The size and shape of tooth crowns and the presence or absence of lateral cusplets on either side of the central tooth crown are among the more commonly referenced morphological odontological characters. These characters are also the focus of renewed scrutiny with respect to phylogenetic and taxonomic importance. Here we document the teeth and dentition of an adult Porbeagle Shark (Lamna nasus) exhibiting an atypical number of tooth cusplets and tooth files. We present and comment on the morphological variability of teeth within a single tooth file and illustrate the presence and developmental sequence of a putatively aberrant symphyseal tooth file. Collectively, these observations highlight the importance of understanding natural intraspecific variation in morphological dental features if they are to be used in taxonomic identification or as phylogenetic characters.
